name: Oxycodone
summary: A full mu-opioid agonist with high oral bioavailability, available as immediate-release for acute pain and abuse-deterrent extended-release for chronic pain.
mechanism: Full agonist at mu-opioid receptors, inhibiting pain transmission; the CYP2D6 metabolite oxymorphone is itself a potent mu agonist.

pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic (CYP3A4 to noroxycodone; CYP2D6 to oxymorphone, active)

dosing.adult: 5–10 mg PO q4–6h PRN (IR); extended-release 10 mg q12h for around-the-clock chronic pain, titrated to effect

safety.pregnancy: Chronic use causes neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome
warnings: Black box: addiction, abuse, and misuse — risk of opioid use disorder
Black box: life-threatening respiratory depression — especially in opioid-naive patients and with CNS depressants
Black box: accidental ingestion and overdose (especially in children) can be fatal
Black box: neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome with prolonged use during pregnancy
ER tablets must be swallowed whole — crushing turns q12h dosing into an immediate-release overdose
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels; inducers lower efficacy
monitoring: Signs of misuse — prescription drug monitoring program review
safety.overdose: Respiratory depression, miosis, coma; naloxone reverses opioid effects (may require repeat doses)

clinicalPearls: Higher oral bioavailability than morphine (~60–87% vs ~30%) — roughly 1.5–2× the oral potency of morphine
ER tablets are q12h and must never be crushed or chewed — that converts the formulation into an immediate-release overdose
good: Moderate-to-severe pain needing reliable oral bioavailability; ER for around-the-clock chronic pain.
bad: Opioid-naive patients without a plan, respiratory compromise, or anyone who might tamper with ER tablets.

provenance.notes: Curated from standard neurology/pharmacology references. Values omitted where not confidently known — nothing invented.
